episode_title: Warum wir das Zuhören verlernen – Rolf Schmiel

real_qa.q: What is Rolf Schmiel's approach to improving conversation quality in professional and personal contexts?
real_qa.r: Schmiel emphasizes that most people believe they are excellent communicators, but genuine good conversation requires real time and engagement. His key advice is to first take care of yourself psychologically, then approach the other person with genuine curiosity. When a partner or colleague arrives stressed, they will likely hit a wall. Instead, taking time together—sharing tea or another ritual—and asking genuinely how they are doing leads to much better communication. He states that trying to override the other person's needs and hoping to be understood accomplishes nothing.
real_qa.requete: Rolf Schmiel good conversation quality approach

real_qa.q: How does smartphone visibility affect conversation quality according to research cited in Schmiel's book?
real_qa.r: When a smartphone is visible in the communication field or on the table, it reduces the quality of conversation unconsciously because you signal that something else is more important for communication than the other person. Schmiel recommends asking people to put their phone away so you can focus on the conversation. He cites this as a favorite tip celebrated by journalists because it works for flirting, business, and all other situations.

real_qa.q: What does Rolf Schmiel mean by 'digital hangover' and how does it relate to AI avatars?
real_qa.r: The digital hangover is the reaction following the initial rush of digital technology. People felt that through the digital world everything was possible—every product, information, and contact became accessible quickly. However, the reality is now becoming dramatic: within two years, in Zoom conferences you won't know whether you are communicating with a person or an AI-generated avatar costing 10 dollars per month. The speed of AI avatar development is so fast that what was science fiction is now becoming standard. When you cannot distinguish which of 12 people in a Zoom call are bots, this creates a crisis of trust.
real_qa.requete: Rolf Schmiel digital hangover AI avatars

real_qa.q: What concrete post-conversation technique does Schmiel use to maintain relationship continuity?
real_qa.r: Schmiel takes notes after conversations to remember specific details about each person and what was discussed. This allows him to reconnect precisely when he speaks with someone again—he knows exactly when he last spoke with them and where to pick up. For example, if someone recently became a parent, he can immediately ask about their child. This method works well for him whether in regular meetings or occasional connections, and he recommends it as a tip for audiences.
real_qa.requete: Schmiel notes conversation technique remember details

real_qa.q: What is Rolf Schmiel's book 'Vom Glück des guten Gesprächs' structured to provide readers?
real_qa.r: At the end of each chapter, Schmiel's book contains concrete action tips—specific things readers should do. The book includes 15 pages of literature with scientific studies and research to back up the psychological claims, not just opinions from an older man with gray hair. The book addresses communication challenges in both private and professional contexts, showing how listeners have unlearned the skill of listening and how digital changes are affecting human connection.
real_qa.requete: Schmiel Vom Glück des guten Gesprächs book structure

guest.bio_context: Rolf Schmiel has been working as a psychologist since 1999 and holds a PhD in psychology. He has written three Spiegel bestsellers and appeared on television approximately 300 times. He previously hosted a weekly radio column on Bayern 3 (Bavarian Broadcasting) and conducts seminars and coaching for companies. He is married, has a 17-year-old son, and currently lives in Sprockhövel near Bochum in the Ruhr Valley region.
